title: What is a token?
body: Language models do not read words; they read tokens, which are chunks of text such as a whole word, part of a word or a punctuation mark. Limits, speed and pricing for most AI services are measured in tokens, so the same sentence can use more or fewer tokens depending on the model.

title: What is a context window?
body: A context window is the amount of text, counted in tokens, that a language model can take into account at once. If a conversation or document is longer than the window, the model cannot use all of it in a single request.

title: What is an AI hallucination?
body: In AI, a hallucination is a confident-sounding output that is false or not supported by the source material. It happens because language models generate likely text rather than look facts up, which is why important claims should be checked against a source.

title: What is retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)?
body: Retrieval-augmented generation lets a language model look up relevant documents first and then write its answer using them. It is a common way to ground answers in current or private information without retraining the model.

title: Prompting or fine-tuning?
body: Fine-tuning means training an already trained model further on extra data so it behaves differently or specialises in a task. Prompting leaves the model unchanged and only changes the instructions you give it, which is usually quicker and cheaper to try first.

title: What is a transformer?
body: The transformer is the neural network design behind most modern language models. Its key idea is attention, which lets the model weigh how relevant each part of the input is to every other part. It was introduced in 2017 in the paper 'Attention Is All You Need'.

title: What is an AI agent?
body: In AI, an agent is a system that observes its environment and takes actions to reach a goal. In current language-model products the word usually means a model that can use tools, such as search or code, over several steps instead of answering once.

title: What is prompt injection?
body: Prompt injection is an attack where text given to a language model, for example inside a web page or document it reads, contains instructions that try to override the ones its developer intended. It is listed among the main security risks for applications built on language models.

title: What is model distillation?
body: Knowledge distillation trains a smaller 'student' model to imitate the outputs of a larger 'teacher' model. The aim is a model that is cheaper and faster to run while keeping much of the larger model's ability.

title: What is an embedding?
body: An embedding turns text, images or other data into a list of numbers so that items with similar meaning end up close together. Search, recommendations and retrieval systems use embeddings to find related content by meaning rather than by exact words.

title: What is prompt engineering?
body: Prompt engineering is the practice of wording the instructions and examples given to an AI model to get better results. Common techniques include giving examples, stating the format you want and asking the model to work step by step.

title: What is RLHF?
body: Reinforcement learning from human feedback trains a model using people's judgements of its answers. Humans rank or rate outputs, a reward model learns those preferences, and the language model is then adjusted to produce answers people rate more highly.
source: Wikipedia: Reinforcement learning from human feedback

title: What does multimodal mean?
body: A multimodal model handles more than one kind of data, such as text, images, audio or video, in the same system. For example, it can answer a question about a photo or describe what is said in an audio clip.
